big: Every adviser hears the same objections: small caps did 30%, I will do it myself, it sounds boring. A good reply is not an argument. It is a small piece of arithmetic the client can check.

lines: Small caps gave 30% a year. Why would I take 12% from a multi-asset fund?
Which three years was the 30%, and what did the next three do? Let us line up the whole ten years, not the best slice of it.
Fine. But then I will buy gold and debt funds myself and skip the fund.
You can. First let us price what each rebalance costs you.

alt: Two made-up ten-year lines: a small cap fund and a multi-asset fund with their deepest falls
caps: Made-up decade, not real data. Small caps: +40%, +48%, +36% in the first three years.
That is about 41% a year, the kind of number people quote. Then come falls of 36% and 18%.
The multi-asset fund never has a spectacular year, and never a terrible one either.
Ten years: small caps ₹394, about 14.7% a year, fall 48%. Multi-asset ₹297, about 11.5%, fall 2%.

alt: Two bars comparing the yearly tax cost of rebalancing three funds by hand and doing it inside a multi-asset fund
caps: A ₹1 crore portfolio of three funds drifts. To fix it, you sell ₹8 lakh of equity.
Assume 40% of that sale is gain: ₹3.2 lakh. Long-term gains are taxed at 12.5% above ₹1.25 lakh a year.
Tax: about ₹24,375 for this one rebalance, plus any exit load. Inside the fund, the investor pays none.
Five such years: about ₹1.2 lakh. The harder cost is nerve: rebalancing means buying equity in a crash.

title: A good reply
stops: Ask for the client's own worst month
Promise it will beat small caps
Tell her small caps are a bad idea
alt: A shield with true and false ways to answer a client's objection
caps: Answer with a number the client can check, not with a lecture.
Compare falls as well as returns. Ask for the client's own worst month and anchor on it.
Never promise that the fund will beat small caps, and never tell the client small caps are bad.

intro: Assumed figures for a ₹20 lakh portfolio. Use the client's own memory of March 2026 instead.
rows: Small cap heavy: a bad month
note: The figures are assumed to show scale. In the meeting, ask what the client felt in the worst month, then size the fund to that.

q: A client says small caps gave 30% a year, so why accept 12% from a multi-asset fund? What is the best first step?
opts: Tell him small caps are too dangerous for any client and refuse to discuss them
Agree, and move his core money to small caps since the past figure is the best guide
Ask which years the 30% covers, then compare the end value and the worst fall
Promise that the multi-asset fund will beat small caps over his next five years
why: A flat refusal ignores his goal. Small caps have a role, in a limited satellite, so a lecture does not help.
A past return from a best window is a weak guide. The deep falls that came with it are part of the story.
A quoted return is often a best window. Comparing the whole period, and the fall, gives him something to check.
No one can promise a future ranking. A promise that later fails costs the client's trust.

q: A client's ₹20 lakh portfolio fell 12% in her worst month when mostly in small caps. A multi-asset fund would have fallen about 4% in that month. How much less would she have lost?
opts: About ₹1.6 lakh, since 12% of ₹20 lakh is ₹2.4 lakh and 4% is ₹80,000
About ₹2.4 lakh, since that is the whole loss in the small cap month
About ₹80,000, since that is the loss the multi-asset fund would have had
About ₹8 lakh, since the gap of 8 points applies to the whole ₹1 crore portfolio
why: ₹2,40,000 less ₹80,000 is ₹1,60,000. The gap is 8 points of ₹20 lakh, which is ₹1.6 lakh.
₹2.4 lakh is the small cap loss, not the difference. The multi-asset fund would still have lost something.
₹80,000 is the multi-asset loss. The saving is the small cap loss minus that figure.
The portfolio is ₹20 lakh, not ₹1 crore. Eight points of ₹20 lakh is ₹1.6 lakh.

q: A client says he will hold gold and debt funds himself instead of a multi-asset fund. What is a fair response?
opts: He cannot, because SEBI does not allow a person to hold gold and debt funds together
He can, but each rebalance may bring tax and exit load, and a crash tests nerve
He should, because rebalancing by hand is simple and never leads to any tax at all
He should never rebalance, since leaving the funds alone is always better in the end
why: Nothing stops an individual from holding several funds. It is a matter of cost and discipline, not permission.
It is possible, but a rebalance is a sale, and the real test is buying equity after a fall. The cost depends on size.
Selling units to rebalance is a taxable event, so the claim of no tax at all is wrong for most sales.
Without rebalancing the mix drifts. After a big rally, equity may dominate and the risk will have risen.

q: A client says a multi-asset fund is boring. What is the most useful reply?
opts: Agree, and drop the multi-asset fund because he should not hold what bores him
Say boring funds always beat exciting ones, so he should not worry about it
Say nothing, since a client's feelings about a fund have no place in planning
Core money should compound steadily; keep excitement for a small satellite
why: Boredom is not a reason to drop a core holding. A satellite can answer the wish for excitement.
Boring does not always beat exciting. A sweeping promise like that cannot be kept in every period.
Feelings drive behaviour, and behaviour drives results. A plan should account for what the client can hold.
Core money is meant to compound quietly. A small satellite gives room for conviction bets, within a cap.

pts: Compare drawdowns and the whole period, not just a best window: a 40% a year start can hide a fall of nearly 50%.
Doing it yourself means tax and exit load on each rebalance, and nerve in a crash. The cost grows with the portfolio.
Boring is the point for core money. Anchor the talk on the client's own worst month.
